problems.title: Stretch plus shear: F to fiber stretch
problems.setup: A block deforms by x₁ = 1.2X₁ + 0.5X₂, x₂ = X₂, x₃ = X₃ (all lengths in the same units). Work in the reference basis e₁, e₂, e₃.

parts.ask: Find the volume ratio J = det F.
sol: F is upper triangular, so J = 1.2 · 1 · 1 = 1.2

parts.ask: Find the Green-Lagrange shear component E₁₂.
Find the stretch λ of the material fiber initially along N = (e₁ + e₂)/√2 (3 significant figures).
The small strain tensor gives ε₁₂ = ½(H₁₂ + H₂₁). How does it compare with E₁₂ = 0.3?
sol: H = F − I has H₁₁ = 0.2, H₁₂ = 0.5
E = ε + ½HᵀH, with ½(HᵀH)₁₂ = ½(0.2 · 0.5) = 0.05

problems.x: C = FᵀF carries all length information, so any fiber stretch follows from λ² = N·CN.

problems.title: Large rotation and the small strain trap
problems.setup: A body deforms by x₁ = −2X₂, x₂ = X₁, x₃ = X₃. Rotations are positive counterclockwise about e₃.

parts.ask: Find J = det F.
Find the Green-Lagrange component E₂₂.
sol: E₂₂ = 1.5, from a fiber stretch of 2 along e₂

parts.ask: Give the polar decomposition F = RU.
parts.a: U = diag(1, 2, 1), R = 90° rotation about e₃
w: U = diag(2, 1, 1), R = −90° rotation about e₃
U = I, R = F itself as a pure rotation
U = diag(1, 4, 1), R = 45° rotation about e₃
sol: R maps e₁ to e₂: a 90° counterclockwise rotation

parts.ask: The small strain tensor ε = ½(H + Hᵀ) gives ε₁₁ = ε₂₂ = −1 here. Explain the discrepancy with E.
parts.a: Linear strain is valid only for small displacement gradients, including small rotations. A 90° rotation makes H large, so ε reports a spurious shrinkage of 100%, while E = ½(UᵀU − I) depends only on the stretch U and is unaffected by R.
sol: E = ½(C − I) is invariant to rigid rotation since C = UᵀRᵀRU = U²
Use E (or U) whenever rotations are finite

problems.x: Green-Lagrange strain depends only on U, so it measures pure stretch regardless of the rotation R.

problems.title: 3D stress state to yield check
problems.setup: At a point, σ₁₁ = 50 MPa, σ₂₂ = −30 MPa, σ₃₃ = 20 MPa, σ₁₂ = 30 MPa, σ₁₃ = σ₂₃ = 0. The material has yield stress σ_y = 95 MPa in uniaxial tension.

parts.ask: Find the largest principal stress σ₁.
sol: e₃ is principal with σ = 20 MPa

parts.ask: Find the absolute maximum shear stress.
sol: It acts on planes at 45° to the 1 and 3 principal directions

parts.ask: Find the von Mises stress (1 decimal).
Compare the Tresca and von Mises predictions with σ_y = 95 MPa.
parts.a: Tresca predicts yield; von Mises predicts elastic
w: von Mises predicts yield; Tresca predicts elastic
sol: von Mises: 87.2 MPa < 95 MPa, so elastic
Tresca is the more conservative criterion, by a factor of up to 2/√3 ≈ 1.155

problems.x: Principal stresses give τ_max = (σ₁ − σ₃)/2 and σ_vm directly, and Tresca is the more conservative of the two yield checks.

problems.title: Traction on an oblique plane and objectivity
problems.setup: The Cauchy stress at a point is σ = [[30, 0, 15],[0, 60, 0],[15, 0, −30]] MPa. Consider the plane with unit normal n = (2, 1, 2)/3.

parts.ask: Find the magnitude of the traction vector t = σn (2 decimals).
Find the normal stress σ_n = n·σn.
Find the shear stress magnitude on the plane (2 decimals).
A rigid rotation Q is superposed on the deformed body (x* = Qx + c). How does the Cauchy stress transform?
sol: Traction is a spatial vector: t* = Qt on the rotated normal n* = Qn
t* = σ*n* gives Qσn = σ*Qn for all n
So σ* = QσQᵀ: Cauchy stress is objective

problems.x: Cauchy's formula t = σn gives the full traction on any plane, and σ rotates as QσQᵀ under a superposed rigid motion.

problems.title: Plane strain Hooke's law and bulk modulus
problems.setup: A steel part (E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.25) is held so that ε₃₃ = 0 (plane strain). In-plane stresses are σ₁₁ = 100 MPa, σ₂₂ = 50 MPa, with all shears zero.

parts.ask: Find the out-of-plane stress σ₃₃.
Find ε₁₁ in microstrain (1 decimal).
Find the volumetric strain ε₁₁ + ε₂₂ + ε₃₃ in microstrain using the bulk modulus.
What happens to σ₃₃ and K as ν approaches 1/2?
parts.a: K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)) grows without bound, so the material becomes incompressible and tr ε goes to zero. The constraint stress σ₃₃ = ν(σ₁₁ + σ₂₂) rises to the in-plane mean, (σ₁₁ + σ₂₂)/2.

problems.x: In plane strain the constraint supplies σ₃₃ = ν(σ₁₁ + σ₂₂), and the mean stress over K gives the volume change directly.

problems.title: Confined compression and the constrained modulus
problems.setup: An aluminum cylinder (E = 70 GPa, ν = 1/3) sits in a rigid frictionless die so that ε₂₂ = ε₃₃ = 0. An axial stress σ₁₁ = −60 MPa is applied. Use σ = λ tr(ε) I + 2με.

parts.ask: Find the Lamé constant λ.
Find the constrained modulus M = σ₁₁/ε₁₁.
Find the axial strain ε₁₁ in microstrain (1 decimal).
Find the lateral die pressure stress σ₂₂.

problems.x: Lateral confinement raises the axial stiffness to M = λ + 2μ = E(1 − ν)/((1 + ν)(1 − 2ν)) and induces σ₂₂ = [ν/(1 − ν)]σ₁₁.

problems.title: End-loaded cantilever by Airy function
problems.setup: A cantilever strip occupies 0 ≤ x ≤ L, −c ≤ y ≤ c, unit thickness, clamped at x = L. The end x = 0 carries a shear resultant ∫σ_xy dy = P, and faces y = ±c are traction free. Use σ_xx = φ,yy, σ_yy = φ,xx, σ_xy = −φ,xy with φ = A xy + B xy³. Take P = 10 kN per m thickness, c = 50 mm, L = 1 m.

parts.ask: Which conditions on φ = A xy + B xy³ are satisfied, and what do the faces y = ±c require?
w: ∇⁴φ = 12By ≠ 0, so B = 0; the faces then give A = 0

parts.ask: Apply the end resultant ∫σ_xy dy = P at x = 0. Find B.
Find the maximum bending stress magnitude, at x = L, y = ±c.
Find the maximum shear stress magnitude, at y = 0 (3 decimals).
sol: σ_xy = (3P/(4c))(1 − y²/c²), a parabola peaking at y = 0

problems.x: The Airy solution reproduces beam theory exactly here: σ_xx = Pxy/I and a parabolic shear with peak 3P/(2·2c) at the neutral axis.

problems.title: Strip under tension and bending
problems.setup: A long plate strip −c ≤ y ≤ c, unit thickness, has traction-free faces y = ±c. Its ends carry an axial force N = 200 kN per m and a moment M = 10 kN·m per m (M = ∫σ_xx y dy). Take c = 100 mm and φ = A y² + B y³, with σ_xx = φ,yy, σ_yy = φ,xx, σ_xy = −φ,xy.

parts.ask: Check the field equation and the face conditions for φ = A y² + B y³.
sol: φ is cubic in y, so φ,yyyy = 0 and ∇⁴φ = 0
φ,xx = φ,xy = 0, so the faces are traction free

parts.ask: Find σ_xx on the face y = +c.
sol: N = ∫σ_xx dy = 4Ac, so A = N/(4c) = 5 × 10⁵ Pa
M = ∫σ_xx y dy = 4Bc³, so B = M/(4c³) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa/m

parts.ask: Find σ_xx on the face y = −c.
Find the y location of zero axial stress, in mm (1 decimal).
sol: The tension shifts the neutral line away from the centroid

problems.x: A cubic Airy function gives the exact linear σ_xx = N/(2c) + My/I for a strip with resultant end loads, matching beam theory.

problems.title: Lamé thick cylinder with thin-wall check
problems.setup: A closed-end thick cylinder has inner radius a = 80 mm, outer radius b = 120 mm, internal pressure p = 50 MPa and zero external pressure. Use σ_rr = A − B/r², σ_θθ = A + B/r².

parts.ask: Find the hoop stress at the bore, σ_θθ(a).
sol: σ_rr(a) = −p and σ_rr(b) = 0 give A = pa²/(b² − a²) = 40 MPa, B = Ab²

parts.ask: Find the hoop stress at the outer surface, σ_θθ(b).
Find the Tresca maximum shear stress at the bore.
sol: Bore principals: σ_θθ = 130, σ_zz = pa²/(b² − a²) = 40, σ_rr = −50 MPa

parts.ask: Find the thin-wall hoop estimate p r_m/t using the mean radius r_m = 100 mm.
sol: The Lamé peak of 130 MPa is 4% higher, since b/a = 1.5 is a thick wall

problems.x: The Lamé hoop stress peaks at the bore at p(a² + b²)/(b² − a²), and the thin-wall formula approaches it as t/r shrinks.

problems.title: Pressure vessel with a helical weld
problems.setup: A closed thin-walled cylinder has mean radius R = 500 mm, wall thickness t = 10 mm and internal pressure p = 2 MPa. A helical weld seam runs at 60° to the cylinder axis.

parts.ask: Find the hoop stress σ_θ.
sol: σ_x = pR/(2t) = 50 MPa from the end cap balance

parts.ask: Find the normal stress acting across the weld (1 decimal).
sol: The weld normal is at 60° + 90° = 150° from the axis

parts.ask: Find the shear stress magnitude along the weld (2 decimals).
Which seam orientation carries the smallest normal stress across it?
w: A longitudinal seam, along the axis
A helical seam at 45° to the axis
A helical seam at 60° to the axis
sol: A circumferential seam has its normal along the axis: σ_n = σ_x = 50 MPa
This is the smaller principal stress, the minimum of σ_n over all angles
A longitudinal seam carries the full hoop stress, 100 MPa

problems.x: Hoop stress is twice axial stress in a closed cylinder, so a seam's normal stress rises from pR/(2t) to pR/t as its normal turns toward the hoop direction.

problems.title: Neo-Hookean bar in uniaxial tension
problems.setup: An incompressible neo-Hookean rubber bar, W = (μ/2)(λ₁² + λ₂² + λ₃² − 3) with μ = 0.6 MPa, is stretched to λ = 1.5 along e₁ with free lateral faces.

parts.ask: Find the lateral stretch λ₂ = λ₃ (3 decimals).
sol: Incompressibility: λ λ₂ λ₃ = 1 with λ₂ = λ₃

parts.ask: Find the nominal (first Piola) stress P₁₁ (3 decimals).
sol: σ = −pI + μB, with σ₂₂ = 0 giving p = μ/λ
σ₁₁ = μ(λ² − 1/λ); P₁₁ = σ₁₁/λ = μ(λ − λ⁻²)

parts.ask: Find the Cauchy stress σ₁₁ (2 decimals).
Linear elasticity with E = 3μ and engineering strain 0.5 gives what σ₁₁, and how does it compare?
w: 0.95 MPa, identical to the neo-Hookean value
0.30 MPa, a third of the neo-Hookean value
1.80 MPa, about twice the neo-Hookean value
sol: Both models share the slope 3μ at λ = 1 and diverge as λ grows

problems.x: For incompressible neo-Hookean tension, σ₁₁ = μ(λ² − 1/λ) and P₁₁ = μ(λ − λ⁻²), both with initial slope E = 3μ.

problems.title: Neo-Hookean balloon pressure peak
problems.setup: A spherical neo-Hookean membrane (incompressible, shear modulus μ = 0.3 MPa) has unstretched radius R = 50 mm and thickness H = 1 mm. It inflates equibiaxially with hoop stretch λ = r/R under internal pressure p.

parts.ask: Combine membrane balance with the neo-Hookean equibiaxial stress. What is p(λ)?
sol: Thickness h = H/λ² and r = λR; balance: p = 2σh/r

parts.ask: Find the stretch at the pressure maximum (3 decimals).
Find the maximum pressure in kPa (2 decimals).
The balloon is inflated under pressure control. What happens once p reaches p_max?
w: The balloon deflates back to radius R
The radius settles at a new stable stretch
sol: Past λ = 7^(1/6), p(λ) falls monotonically toward zero
Holding p = p_max then exceeds the equilibrium pressure, so λ keeps growing
Strain stiffening models such as Gent or Ogden supply a rising branch that arrests it

problems.x: Thinning and growing radius give the neo-Hookean balloon a pressure peak at λ = 7^(1/6), beyond which pressure control drives a runaway inflation.

problems.title: Material derivative and continuity in 1D stretching
problems.setup: A spatial velocity field is v₁ = x₁/(1 + t), v₂ = v₃ = 0 (x in m, t in s). At t = 0 the density is uniform, ρ₀ = 1000 kg/m³, and x = X.

parts.ask: Find the local rate ∂v₁/∂t at x₁ = 2 m, t = 1 s.
Find the material acceleration a₁ = Dv₁/Dt at the same point.
sol: a₁ = −0.5 + 0.5 = 0: each particle moves at constant speed

parts.ask: Use continuity to find ρ at t = 1 s.
sol: Dρ/Dt = −ρ∇·v = −ρ/(1 + t), so ρ = ρ₀/(1 + t)

parts.ask: Give the Lagrangian description of this motion and confirm the density with J.
parts.a: Integrating dx₁/dt = x₁/(1 + t) from x₁ = X₁ gives x₁ = X₁(1 + t), so F₁₁ = J = 1 + t. Mass conservation ρJ = ρ₀ gives ρ = ρ₀/(1 + t), matching the Eulerian result.
sol: x₁ = X₁(1 + t), V₁ = X₁ constant in time, so A₁ = 0

problems.x: The material derivative adds the convective term v·∇v to ∂v/∂t, and continuity Dρ/Dt + ρ∇·v = 0 is the Eulerian form of ρJ = ρ₀.

problems.title: Steady stagnation flow: convective acceleration
problems.setup: A steady plane velocity field is v₁ = kx₁, v₂ = −kx₂, v₃ = 0 with k = 3 s⁻¹ (x in m). Evaluate quantities at the point x = (1, 2, 0) m.

parts.ask: Find the acceleration component a₂.
Find the acceleration magnitude |a| (2 decimals).
What does continuity say about this flow?
w: ∇·v = −k, so particles compress at rate k
sol: Dρ/Dt = −ρ∇·v = 0: each particle keeps its density

parts.ask: Decompose L = ∇v = D + W. Which statement holds?
parts.a: W = 0, so the motion is irrotational
w: D = 0, so the motion is a pure rigid spin
W = diag(k, −k), the spin rate tensor
D = W, both equal to L/2
sol: D = ½(L + Lᵀ) = L and W = ½(L − Lᵀ) = 0
Fluid elements stretch along e₁ and shorten along e₂ at rate k

problems.x: A steady field still accelerates particles through the convective term (∇v)v, and tr L = ∇·v sets the volume change rate.

problems.title: Constrained bar and bimaterial thermal stress
problems.setup: A steel bar (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K), length L = 1 m, is heated uniformly by ΔT = 50 K. Later, the same steel bar is placed side by side with an aluminum bar (E = 70 GPa, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ /K) of equal length and equal cross-sectional area, both bars joined at each end to a rigid plate so they share one axial strain, and the pair is heated by 50 K with no external load.

parts.ask: Both ends of the steel bar are fixed to rigid walls. Find its stress.
Now one wall has a 0.2 mm gap. Find the steel stress after heating.
sol: Free expansion: αΔT L = 600 × 10⁻⁶ (1000 mm) = 0.6 mm
Blocked part: 0.6 − 0.2 = 0.4 mm, a strain of 400 µε

parts.ask: Find the common strain of the bonded steel-aluminum pair, in microstrain (1 decimal).
sol: Equal areas and zero net force: E_s(ε − α_sΔT) + E_a(ε − α_aΔT) = 0

parts.ask: Find the stress in the steel bar of the pair (2 decimals).
sol: Force balance gives σ_a = −28.52 MPa in the aluminum

problems.x: Thermal stress comes from blocked thermal strain: σ = E(ε − αΔT), with the total strain set by the constraint or by force balance.

problems.title: Rule of mixtures for a glass/epoxy lamina
problems.setup: A unidirectional glass/epoxy lamina has fiber volume fraction V_f = 0.5, fiber modulus E_f = 72 GPa and matrix modulus E_m = 3 GPa. Fibers and matrix are perfectly bonded.

parts.ask: Find the longitudinal modulus E₁ by the rule of mixtures.
sol: Equal strain in both phases (parallel, Voigt)

parts.ask: Find the transverse modulus E₂ by the inverse rule of mixtures (2 decimals).
sol: Equal stress in both phases (series, Reuss)

parts.ask: Under a load along the fibers, find the fraction of the load carried by the fibers (2 decimals).
How does the series estimate E₂ relate to the true transverse modulus?
parts.a: It is a lower bound, matrix dominated
w: It is an upper bound, fiber dominated
It is exact for any fiber packing
sol: Uniform stress is the Reuss lower bound on stiffness
Half the volume is compliant matrix, which governs 1/E₂
Halpin-Tsai gives a closer estimate, above 5.76 GPa

problems.x: Fibers in parallel give the stiff, fiber dominated E₁ = V_fE_f + V_mE_m, while the series model gives the matrix dominated lower bound for E₂.
